title: Contrasts: Pero, Sino, and Sino que

sections.content:
You know *pero* ('but') from A1. New here: when the first part is negative and the second part corrects it, Spanish uses *sino* or *sino que*:

• **Pero**: Adds a contrast, nuance, or limitation to a statement (positive or negative):
  *Estudié mucho, pero no aprobé.* (I studied a lot, but didn't pass.)
• **Sino**: used **after a negative clause** to correct one element (*not X, but rather Y*):
  *No quiero té, sino café.* (I don't want tea, but coffee.)
  *No es español, sino portugués.* (He is not Spanish, but Portuguese.)
• **Sino que**: Used when the correction contains a **conjugated verb**:
  *No fue al cine, sino que se quedó en casa estudiando.* (He didn't go to the movies, but rather stayed home studying.)

sections.title: Rules and Patterns
rows: Es caro, pero de buena calidad.
No solo trabaja, sino que también estudia.

items.spanish: No fuimos en avión, sino en tren.
items.english: We didn't go by plane, but by train.

items.spanish: No perdí el documento, sino que se lo entregué al director.
items.english: I didn't lose the document, but rather handed it to the director.

items.spanish: El examen era difícil, pero todos aprobamos.
items.english: The exam was difficult, but we all passed.

sections.content: Formula: Negative clause + noun/adj = **sino**. Negative clause + conjugated verb = **sino que**.
